Hi Ani,

Just looking at your code, it looks like there is a mismatch between the order of species in the colors and the PCA scores you are giving the plot function. species.phypca comes from species.means while species.subfamily comes from EcoBehSpecies.matched$Subfamily.

What I would do is inspect the rownames of the scores within species.phypca$x and make sure that the colors you provide match the species order as you expect them to so the colors match up when using plot().

Regarding your legend, I saw some colors repeated, implying that you may need to provide the legend function the levels and not a factor. Getting the legend you want may also involve reordering the levels manually, I think they are usually listed alphabetically within a factor. Or you may be able to provide text and colors/color codes yourself and make the legend manually.

Best,
Bryan

GPA with sliding is:

Translation, scale, rotation, slide. Find mean shape, Iterate. It will work with all semilandmarks, though I find it a bit more stable with at least one fixed point. However, recall that the original 1997 paper introducing the approach used all sliding landmarks on the corpus callosum.

Hi Jimmy,

For estimating loss of biomass I might simply look at area loss; I.e. measure before and after (or group means) of area by making outlines in something like imagej.

If you are interested in shape differences, I think your problem is tricky because you won’t have landmarks (homologous points between specimens). One approach you might look into is Fourier shape analysis, which for 2D seems fairly straightforward.

Katie

Jayme,

That article was written quite a few years before we published the geomorph and RRPP software packages, so the routine was written by hand by me. However, you can approximate our procedure by reclassifying performing the disparity analysis you used, but grouping all adults as one group and neonates as another group (in other words, calculating and comparing the disparities between two groups). The disparity values within Adults and Neonates is the squared version of the values we used back in 2010, and the pairwise comparison of these values via RRPP is the most appropriate approach for comparing whether adult disparity is greater or less than neonate disparity.

One final difference is that in our 2010 paper we used the mean adult and mean juvenile in the analysis. However, you only have 3 groups, so that would likely reduce any statistical power for the test in your particular case.

Hope this helps.

Unfortunately, you do not have the required replication to perform the test (or any test really).

For trajectory analysis, you either need multiple individuals per level to define each trajectory (as described in the original Collyer and Adams 2007 procedure), or you require multiple, replicate full trajectories in each group (as described in the Adams and Cerney 2007 motion trajectory procedure). Either way, one requires replication of trajectory units or individuals used to describe those units.

>From your email, it seems you have a single juvenile and a single adult per species ‘trajectory’.  With this, all one can do is draw lines between Juv—Adult in morphospace to visualize ontogeny. But statistical tests like those in trajectory analysis are not possible, as there is no replication in the study design. As with all statistical analyses, trajectory analysis requires replication to estimate variation against which observed patterns may be compared.

Sorry.

messages.subject: Compare expected mean shape using pairwise
messages.subject_clean: Compare expected mean shape using pairwise
messages.body_plain:
I have shape data for individuals aged 6, 7, and 10 years, which includes both sexes. I performed fit1 <- lm.rrpp(shape ~ sex*age) and want to test for statistical signiciance of shape differences of the expected mean shape between sexes at each age group. Here is how I did it:

gp <- interaction(sex, age)
pw <- pairwise(fit1, groups = gp)
summary(pw, confidence = 0.95, test.type = "dist")

This will return significance of shape differences at ages 6, 7, and 10 years. Since I have established a linear model of shape and age, I am also interested in predicting shape at ages 8 and 9, and compare sexual dimorphism of shapes at these two ages. Is there a way to do this in geomorph/RRPP?

A solution is to permute group labels 1000 times and run lm.rrpp with iter=1 each time. This will create a distribution of Procrustes distance at whichever ages of interest and just calculate the number of times the permuted PD is larger than the observed (i.e., p value). Please let me know if this is a valid alternative. But I do want to do this inside geomorph/RRPP.

Thank you.
Kieran
